old_caption: The video captures a close-up view of several crayons arranged vertically on a white surface. The crayons are of various colors, including orange, yellow, green, black, blue, pink, and red. Some of the crayons have been used, as evidenced by the melted wax at their tips, which has dripped down onto the surface below. A black object, possibly a cup or container, is positioned above the crayons and remains stationary throughout the video. The background remains consistently white throughout the video, emphasizing the vibrant colors of the crayons and the contrast created by the melted wax. There are no animals or characters present in the scene, and the focus remains solely on the crayons and the black object above them. The camera maintains a steady position, providing a clear and detailed view of the objects.

caption: The video captures a white vertical surface holding twelve crayons standing tip-down in three loose clusters. A left group of red-brown, yellow, green and black sits beside a middle group of orange, yellow, dark blue and orange Crayola, with a right group of pink, yellow Crayola, peach and black. Colored drag streaks in red, yellow, green and black mark the surface beneath the left cluster, and orange and yellow trails run under the middle cluster. The crayons and these streaks appear to hold their positions relative to the frame throughout the segment, with no visible translation or rotation among them. A dark cup-shaped object intrudes from the top-left corner, partly out of frame at the start. Over the course of the clip this object drifts gradually rightward and downward. It increases its extent within the frame and shifts its position against the white background. The view stays continuous with no cut, and this slow movement is the most prominent change while the arranged crayons hold their places.

endpoints are normal, not physical errors. Do not add unseen causes, onset, stopping or outcomes.
An internal editing cut is not evidence of physical motion connecting the views.

Check identification before physical interpretation: a reflection is not a separate actor;
a powder/smoke/liquid outline or shadow is not automatically the boundary of a solid object;
an apparent change caused by occlusion/viewpoint is not automatically material deformation.
Do not claim contact, bending, compression, melting, disintegration or structural recovery unless
the appropriate material/surface itself provides visible evidence. Do not infer a force or earlier
collision just because the visible configuration would be compatible with it.

camera tracking. A single visible texture/seam does not prove spin. Avoid unnecessary absolute
claims of stillness, no motion, no camera motion or 'exactly' synchronized changes.

processes. Avoid deleting the real process merely because its cause lies outside the cropped window.
